Rodrigo, welcome to the show. I've asked sixty lawyers this question, and only three said yes. Did you always want to be a lawyer?
Honestly, no. I started in Salvador, almost by accident, and in my first week I was thrown in at the deep end: a client meeting, alone.
That sounds familiar. On my first day as a reporter, my editor sent me to a murder trial on my own. So how did you learn the ropes?
I had a mentor, an older partner. Not only did he make me write every contract twice, he made me explain every clause out loud.
And when did all that start to pay off?
Only after I moved to São Paulo did I really see it. Two years later, I landed my first international client. That was my breakthrough.
You tried litigation for a while, and then you pivoted back to corporate work. Why?
I do enjoy a good argument, believe me. But rarely have I felt as useful as when a deal closes. That's where I thrive.
Last question, and it's for our listeners in law school. How do they make a name for themselves?
Lay the groundwork early, and find a niche you actually enjoy. Little did I know, in Salvador, that those boring first years would be the most rewarding.

I've produced interview podcasts for eleven years, and I can usually tell in the first minute whether a guest is going to work. It has nothing to do with how famous they are. The guests who struggle are the ones who give us their resume: dates, job titles, the names of firms. Listeners forget all of that in seconds. The guests who work tell us about one moment. The week they were thrown in at the deep end. The mentor who said something they still remember. The decision that looked wrong at the time and paid off ten years later. Rarely do people remember a list, but they almost always remember a scene. So before every recording, I give my guests one piece of homework. Choose three moments from your career, and practice telling each one in under a minute. Not only does it make the interview better, it makes them sound more confident, because they are no longer searching for what to say.

When I retired last year, a young associate asked me what I would do differently. I had to think about it for a long time. Little did I know, when I started, how much of this job is about people, and how little of it is about the law. In my first year, I was sure that the best lawyer was the one who knew the most cases. I worked eighty hours a week, and I thought that was enough. It wasn't. Only when I lost a client I had represented for six years did I understand why. He told me he never knew what I was thinking. I had never once asked him what worried him. After that, I changed the way I worked. I called clients when there was no problem. I explained my advice in plain words. I did keep working hard, of course, but I started listening first. My practice doubled in the next five years. So my answer to the associate was simple. Learn the law, yes. But learn the client first.
